name: Nikhil Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy soft drinks, bottled water, coffee and catering supplies for Harbourline, a family-run firm that delivers to cafes, canteens and vending machines. I start at eight with the delivery plan, then I spend the morning on the phone with bottlers and coffee roasters. In summer the water orders go through the roof, and in winter it's coffee and hot chocolate. What I like most is a clean week where every van leaves full and nothing's short.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Meera runs a small daycare from our home, six children on a good day. We have Arjun, twelve, and Tara, nine, and a mortgage on a three-bedroom house. I'm 43, and I only moved to buying from van driving seven years ago, so I'm still the junior of the two buyers, and the owner's nephew, Rahul, is the other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fine by me. At work I'd say let's keep doing what works, because a good phone call beats a clever gadget. With friends I'd say hard work and a straight handshake still count for a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel fairly settled. Harbourline is family-run, the owner, Mr Patel, treats us decently, and the cafes and canteens need drinks whatever happens. Money is tight with the mortgage, but I wouldn't lose sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I do now. I'd keep paying the mortgage and put about two hundred a month into the savings. I'd use the AI chatbot a few times a week, as I do now, to draft emails and check supplier prices, and I'd keep helping Meera with the daycare paperwork on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels pretty calm. If anything, it feels familiar, which is a good thing at my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say is the biggest risk to Harbourline?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A big chain buying out one of our main bottlers, or one of our big customers like the hospital canteen switching supplier. Those are worries that have nothing to do with AI. Mr Patel is the sort who would tell us if it got serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you actually use AI for now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few things. I ask it to write polite emails when a bottler is late, and I ask it to compare two price lists side by side. I don't trust it with the final numbers, so I check them myself. It's like a fast intern who sometimes gets things wrong.

say: I'd say **hard work** and a straight handshake still count for a lot.
I'd tell colleagues a good phone call beats a clever gadget.
think: I'd feel **fairly settled**, since a family-run firm and the cafes need drinks whatever happens.
Money is tight with the mortgage, but I wouldn't lose sleep.
do: Keep going and put **two hundred a month** into savings.
Use the chatbot a few times a week for emails and price checks.
Help Meera with the daycare paperwork on Sundays.
feel: Pretty **calm**, and familiar, which is good at my age.
S0.quote: Let's keep doing what works, because a good phone call beats a clever gadget.
fieldNote: Feels secure in a **family-run** firm, though money is tight with the mortgage.
Uses the chatbot like a fast intern and checks every number himself.

steps.text: Keep buying drinks and coffee for the Harbourline vans
Use the chatbot to draft emails and compare price lists
Put two hundred a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good if it makes us faster, so let's use it carefully. At work I'd say we should try it on the boring bits first. With friends I'd say jobs will change, and people should learn something useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel uneasy but not scared. A family firm moves slowly, and Mr Patel won't swap people for software overnight. But the big distributors will, and they'd squeeze our prices, so I'd watch that carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly, instead of using them a bit. I'd ask Mr Patel if I can set up an automatic reorder for the bottled water and coffee, since those orders repeat every week. I'd also keep up my savings and take a short course in inventory management, evenings, at the local college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a change in the weather. You put on a coat and carry on, but you pay more attention to the forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Mr Patel's loyalty to you have limits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Loyalty, yes, but he's a businessman. If a big rival cut prices by ten percent because of software, he'd have to follow or lose customers. He'd keep family first, and I'm not family, so I try to be useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your tasks do you expect software to take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reordering and price comparisons. That's most of what the system does at the moment, and a smarter system would do it without me. What it can't do is know that Mrs Okafor at the canteen doesn't like deliveries before nine, or that a driver's van is in the garage.

say: I'd say it's good if it makes us **faster**, so use it carefully.
I'd say try it on the boring jobs first.
think: I'd feel **uneasy but not scared**, since a family firm moves slowly.
The big distributors will use software and squeeze our prices.
do: Learn the tools properly and set up **automatic reorders** for water and coffee.
Take an evening inventory management course.
feel: Like a **change in the weather**: put on a coat and carry on.
S1.quote: What it can't do is know that Mrs Okafor at the canteen doesn't like deliveries before nine, or that a driver's van is in the garage.
fieldNote: Moves from **suspicion** to a plan: learn the tools and set up automatic reordering himself.
Frames his value as local knowledge of customers and drivers.

steps.text: Learn to use the AI tools properly, not just now and then
Set up automatic reordering for water and coffee
Take an evening inventory management course
Keep adding two hundred a month to savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and families should be protected. At work I'd tell Mr Patel we need a plan for every person on the payroll. With friends I'd say we need leaders to put work and families first, not just profit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd lose my job inside two years. A machine can do my ordering, my forecasting and my supplier talks, and it would be cheaper than me. I'm the junior buyer, and Rahul is the owner's nephew, so you can guess who stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything, the Friday takeaway and the cable package, and I'd save six hundred a month. I'd go back to van driving if I had to, because Harbourline will still need drivers for a while. And I'd put some money into a vending machine or two, so I'd have my own small business running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a punch. I'd put on a brave face for Meera and the kids, and then lie awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mr Patel in the first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Mr Patel, you've been good to me, so tell me honestly. Is my job here in two years? If not, can I move to the vans or the warehouse? I'd rather have a straight answer from my boss than a kind one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Meera's daycare fit into the picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The daycare is the steady part. Children need adults, and parents will still want someone they trust. If my wage stopped, Meera's daycare income wouldn't cover the mortgage, but it'd keep food on the table, and that's something.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and families should be protected.
I'd say we need leaders to put work and families ahead of profit.
think: A machine can do my ordering and supplier talks, so I'd lose my job in **two years**.
I'm the junior and Rahul is the owner's nephew.
do: Cut the takeaway and cable and save **six hundred** a month.
Go back to van driving if I have to.
Invest in a vending machine or two for my own small business.
feel: Like a **punch**; a brave face for the family and then awake at night.
S2.quote: I'd rather have a straight answer from my boss than a kind one.
fieldNote: Knows the owner's **nephew** will stay while he goes, and says so without bitterness.
Planning a fallback in van driving and a small vending business.

steps.text: Cut the Friday takeaway and cable package
Save six hundred a month for the mortgage
Ask Mr Patel about moving to the vans or warehouse
Buy a vending machine and put it in a local business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a fair warning, so let's use it well. At work I'd say let's modernise carefully and train people. With friends I'd say don't wait to be told.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be anxious but fairly steady. I'd have time to put some money aside and start something of my own. My worry is being 48 with the kids in their teens, but I could do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the vending side now, maybe with three machines in workplaces I know through Harbourline. I'd save four hundred a month and pay down the mortgage when I can. I'd also learn the AI tools well so that I'm the one who sets up Harbourline's automatic ordering, rather than the one it replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a long walk with a heavy bag. I'd rather start early than carry it last minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years: what's the first thing you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy used machines, spend a year learning what sells, and build a small route. Every machine should clear about eighty a month. After three years I could have eight vending machines, that's six hundred and forty on the side, and a small foot in my own business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Arjun about his future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Arjun to learn a trade or a skill that needs hands, and to study hard anyway. I'd tell him the world changes, and to keep his word and his work ethic, as those still count. And to be curious about the tools, not afraid.

say: I'd say it's a **fair warning**, so let's use it well.
I'd say don't wait to be told.
think: I'd be anxious but **fairly steady**, with time to put money aside and start something of my own.
My worry is being 48 with teenagers.
do: Start a **vending** side route with three machines in workplaces I know.
Learn the AI tools so I set up Harbourline's automatic ordering.
feel: A long walk with a **heavy bag**; better to start early.
S3.quote: After three years I could have eight vending machines, that's six hundred and forty on the side, and a small foot in my own business.
fieldNote: Turns the extra time into a **business plan** with numbers, which is his habit.
Wants to be the person who sets up the automation, not the person replaced.

steps.text: Buy three used vending machines for workplaces I know
Save four hundred a month and overpay the mortgage
Set up Harbourline's automatic ordering myself
Teach Arjun to value a skilled trade and a good name

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, we can plan. At work I'd keep learning and help others. With friends I'd say work hard now, because the next ten years matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel uneasy, but there's time. By 2036 I'd be 53 and the kids would be at university or training. I'd have a bit more than I do now, and robots won't be doing hands-on jobs until 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and build the vending route into something, maybe fifteen machines by year seven. I'd pay the mortgage down well before then. I'd also keep learning the AI tools and taking occasional courses, because a decade of that adds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels manageable. I'd still have a thought in the back of my head, but I'd be sleeping fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years make you complacent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would, honestly. If I think I've got ten years, I'll tell myself I'll start next year. So I'd put the vending machines in the first year, so I'm not waiting. Meera would remind me, and she's not shy about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Tara by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want Tara to have a trade or a profession where she's needed in person, and a church or community that holds her up. If she can run a small business, or care for people, she'd be fine. I'd want her to be kind and brave.

say: I'd say **good**, we can plan, and work hard now.
I'd keep learning and help others at work.
think: I'd feel uneasy but there's **time**, and robots won't do hands-on jobs until 2039.
By 2036 I'd be 53 with the kids at university or training.
do: Build the **vending** route to about fifteen machines by year seven.
Keep taking occasional courses on AI tools.
feel: **Manageable**, with a thought in the back of my head.
S4.quote: If I think I've got ten years, I'll tell myself I'll start next year.
fieldNote: Admits he'd **procrastinate** and builds in his wife to keep him honest.
Wants Tara in work where she's needed in person and part of a community.

steps.text: Put the first vending machines in during year one
Pay the mortgage down well before 2036
Take occasional courses on the AI tools
Help Tara aim for work where she's needed in person

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I couldn't build anything in time, and Meera's daycare alone doesn't cover a mortgage. What would help is apprenticeships for people my age, a fair chance to keep a job in the vans, and easy loans for someone who wants to start a small business.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about what I value. I value a handshake and a promise kept. If a machine does the ordering, I still want a person to look a customer in the eye when something goes wrong.

headlineQuote: If a machine does the ordering, I still want a person to look a customer in the eye when something goes wrong.
portrait: Nikhil, 43, is a **junior buyer** of drinks at Harbourline, with a home daycare wife, two children and a mortgage.
He uses AI now and then like a fast intern, checks everything, and values handshakes and loyalty.
He plans practical steps: automatic ordering, a vending route and a fallback in van driving.
He is calm in mild worlds, alarmed when AGI is two years away, and uneasy in the long runway.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most because he couldn't build anything in time.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** for people his age, a chance to stay in the vans, and easy small-business loans.
